newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CITY BIRD TO RULE IN BRUSSELS LONG-HAUL DESERT.
newsitem.headline: CITY BIRD TO RULE IN BRUSSELS LONG-HAUL DESERT.

text.p: Fledgling airline City Bird said on Wednesday it aimed to become the leading long-haul carrier in Brussels which offered vast potential for transatlantic traffic.
"I see City Bird becoming one of the main, if not the main long-haul airlines flying from Brussels," City Bird president Victor Hasson told Reuters in an interview.
"There's the contract with (tour operator) NUR...there's Brussels which is a desert when it comes to long-haul. It's the right time to give it a try," he said.

He said Belgian flag carrier Sabena should be ruled out as a long-haul carrier partly because it had focused on developing its European hub and passengers were not convinced of the quality of its code-share deal with U.S. carrier Delta Air.
"If we're successful, we'll have 10 times more trumps than Sabena which is bogged down in problems with unions. We have fewer costs, we are more flexible," he said.
City Bird, which will launch on March 27 with a starting capital of $5 million, is 62.5-percent owned by Belgian hotels and leisure group City Hotels which is also run by Hasson.

Operating a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 aircraft which is leased for 18 years, City Bird will offer, via leading Belgian tour operator NUR, flights from Brussels to the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Mexico and Jamaica.
It will also run regular services to Miami, Orlando and Mexico, and to Los Angeles, San Francisco and New York after receiving its second MD-11 in early June.
Hasson said that NUR was filling 65 percent of the first plane but that the second plane would have to lure passengers from scheduled flights.

"The second is more risky...but I'm convinced that there are enough passengers to fill two flights a week to Los Angeles for example. It's just a matter of getting people to know the product," he said.
Asked why no-one else had tried to launch a long-haul carrier in Brussels, Hasson said there were no entrepeneurs in Belgium.
City Bird is Hasson's second adventure in aviation.
He launched EuroBelgian Airlines in late 1991 and sold 90 percent of it to British entrepreneur Richard Branson who started trading it as Virgin Express.
Hasson noted his contract with Branson stipulated he could not launch a rival European regional carrier.
Hasson played down the impact of soaring fuel prices and the dollar rise on the new airline.
"Fuel was already high when we (announced) our tariffs and we're covered for the dollar," he said.
He said there was "good understanding" but no talks with Sabena.

He said City Bird already signed a deal with Swissair, which has 49.5 percent of Sabena, for most of the maintenance, and that it planned deals with Sabena or Belgian Belgavia for handling and catering.
